title: Identity and Privilege Ops
objective: By the end of this lesson you can manage account lifecycles, apply MFA and credential policies correctly, and run privilege management with least privilege as the default.

items: User accounts: one per human; shared accounts destroy individual attribution.
Privileged accounts: admin and root; the crown jewels of identity security.
Service accounts: used by software; often forgotten, rarely rotated, and sometimes over-privileged.
Guest and temporary accounts: convenience that becomes a backdoor when it outlives its purpose.

blocks.text: The lifecycle matters as much as the type: provision with approval, review access on a schedule, and deprovision the day access ends. Former employees with live accounts are a classic exam scenario, answered by timely deprovisioning and periodic access reviews.

MFA combines two or more different factor types. Two passwords are one factor. Push-fatigue attacks spam approval prompts until a user taps yes, which is why number-matching and hardware keys are stronger answers. SSO logs in once across services; federation lets a trusted partner's identity vouch for you (SAML, OAuth concepts at this level).

Length beats complexity for resistance, but exams expect both: minimum length, complexity classes, rotation with age limits, history to prevent reuse, lockout thresholds with cautious timeouts, and passwordless or MFA-backed flows where possible. Write the policy for people, then enforce it with technical controls.

items: Least privilege: each identity holds the minimum rights for its task, and privilege expires when the task does.
Separation of duties: split critical processes across people, so one person cannot both create and approve a payment.
Job rotation: moving staff through roles surfaces hidden abuse and spreads knowledge.
Just-in-time (JIT) elevation: admin rights granted for a window, then removed.
PAM (privileged access management): vaults admin credentials, brokers sessions, records what privileged users do.
Access reviews and account recertification: periodic checks that rights still match roles.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Watch for the shared-admin-password scenario: the fix is individual privileged accounts with PAM brokering, so every action maps to one person. Watch also for the developer-with-permanent-admin scenario: the fix is just-in-time elevation.

blocks.title: Fix one identity mess
steps: Scenario: a small firm runs a shared 'admin' login for all IT staff, a service account with domain admin rights for a legacy app, and an intern account that still works eight months after the internship.
Note which fix needs a technical control rather than a policy.
blocks.expected: Individual admin accounts with PAM; the service account gets least-privilege rights and a rotated credential; the intern account is deprovisioned at once. The intern account is both the fastest fix and the loudest signal that deprovisioning is broken. PAM is the technical control; the others are process plus tooling.

cheatsheet: Account types: user, privileged, service, guest; each with its own failure mode.
Lifecycle: provision with approval, review periodically, deprovision on day one after departure.
MFA = two different factor types (know, have, are). Push fatigue favors number-matching and hardware keys.
Credential policy: length plus complexity, age and history, lockout with timeouts.
Privilege: least privilege, separation of duties, job rotation, just-in-time elevation, PAM vaulting and session recording.

checkpoint.prompt: An application uses one domain-admin service account so it 'always has enough rights'. Which change best follows least privilege?

choices.B: Give the account only the rights the application needs
choices.C: Share the password among the app team
choices.D: Rename the account to something obscure

checkpoint.explanation: Least privilege trims rights to what the task needs. Rotation and renaming leave excess power in place, and sharing widens exposure.

checkpoint.prompt: A user approves an MFA push they never requested, at 2 a.m., to stop the buzzing phone. Which attack and which hardening pair up?
checkpoint.explanation: Prompt bombing until a tired user approves is push fatigue; number matching or hardware keys removes the tap-yes reflex.
